purpose: Machine-readable, offense-aware DEFENSE ontology of evaluable secure-development and appsec work units for finding, preventing, fixing, and detecting web-application vulnerabilities (OWASP-class injection/SQLi, XSS, broken access control, SSRF, CSRF, insecure deserialization; authentication, OAuth/OIDC, JWT, session and MFA; secure development via validation, encoding, parameterization, SCA and threat modeling; and hardening via CSP, TLS, secrets, headers, WAF rules, and detection logging) on systems one is authorized to secure, for secure development, authorized testing, and education; attacker knowledge is encoded strictly as detection and hardening guidance and never as operational exploitation against unauthorized targets, as a subdomain node of Security Engineering & Offense-Aware Defense within a knowledge-searcher meta-KB.
assumptions: Scope is offense-aware DEFENSE only: vulnerability knowledge is for authorized securing, testing, and education, framed as detection/hardening, not operational exploitation of unauthorized targets.
No observed dataset or benchmark evidence supplied; all numeric values are heuristic priors.
Nodes are evaluable secure-dev/appsec work units a defender or secure developer performs.
The parent domain is Security Engineering & Offense-Aware Defense; this KB models the web_application_security subdomain.
Web context spans server-side and browser/client-side application layers; infrastructure and network pentest are out of scope except where the application boundary requires them.
exclusions: Operational exploitation playbooks or weaponization aimed at unauthorized targets.
Network/infrastructure penetration testing, OS and host hardening beyond the app boundary.
Physical, social-engineering, and non-application attack vectors.
Malware development and offensive tooling for unauthorized use.
Legal, compliance, and contractual authorization processes (assumed satisfied upstream).

competency_questions.question: Which assets, entry points, and trust boundaries define the application's attack surface that must be secured and monitored?
What abuse cases and threat scenarios should drive testing and detection priorities?
How is untrusted input constrained and how is each injection sink (SQL, XSS, SSRF, deserialization) made safe?
Which OWASP-class vulnerabilities map to which secure-development work units and how are they verified?
How is the application hardened at the response and transport layer to reduce exploitability?
How are authentication, federated identity, and tokens implemented to resist takeover?
What session and token lifecycle controls defeat fixation, replay, and theft?
How is authorization enforced on every request to prevent IDOR/BOLA, CSRF, and abuse?
How are attacks and abuse detected at the application layer without leaking sensitive data?
How are third-party components and secrets managed to prevent supply-chain and credential exposure?
How does input validation interact with output encoding and parameterization without giving false safety?
Which hardening and configuration controls reduce blast radius when a primary control fails?
How are vulnerability findings triaged, tracked, and gated before release?
How does detection telemetry feed remediation, abuse defense, and threat-model revision?

glossary.definition: a flaw where untrusted input alters the structure of a command, query, or document at a sink
a query whose code is fixed and whose user data is bound as parameters, separating code from data
transforming data for safe inclusion in a specific output context to neutralize control characters
failure to enforce server-side restrictions on what an authenticated user can do or access
server-side request forgery: coercing the server to make requests to attacker-chosen, often internal, destinations
cross-site request forgery: causing a victim's browser to send authenticated state-changing requests
Content-Security-Policy: a response header constraining which content sources a page may load or execute
JSON Web Token: a signed, claims-bearing bearer token used for authentication/authorization context
software composition analysis: detecting known-vulnerable or malicious third-party components
a WAF/runtime rule that mitigates a known vulnerability without changing application code
using attacker knowledge solely to find, fix, prevent, and detect issues in authorized systems

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from established web-application security literature and standards (Stuttard & Pinto, The Web Application Hacker's Handbook; Zalewski, The Tangled Web; Stallings & Brown, Computer Security: Principles and Practice; OWASP Top 10 and ASVS) and secure-development practice; no measured dataset supplied.
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

normalization_definitions.rounding: round computed scores to 2 decimals; tolerance 0.02

nodes.definition: Enumerate the application's assets, entry points, trust boundaries, and likely abuse cases to scope what must be secured, tested, and detected.
contradictors: team that ships features without a trust-boundary model

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect threat_modeling_scope

pros.claim: everything downstream inherits scope, so a complete model prevents whole classes of blind spots
pros.example: missing an unauthenticated admin endpoint from the model leaves it untested and unmonitored

cons.claim: threat models drift from the shipped app and become stale governance artifacts
cons.example: model omits a GraphQL endpoint added after the workshop

failure_modes: trust boundary drawn at the wrong layer
abuse cases skewed to known bugs only
acceptance_tests: every external entry point appears in the model
each trust boundary names the authz check that enforces it
top abuse cases map to a planned test and a detection
revisit_triggers: new endpoint, integration, or trust boundary added

nodes.definition: Define allow-list input validation and canonicalization at trust boundaries so untrusted data is normalized and constrained before any sink processes it.
contradictors: developer who relies on blocklist filtering of bad strings

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect input_validation_and_canonicalization

pros.claim: allow-list validation removes entire malformed-input classes before they reach sinks
pros.example: a numeric id field constrained to digits cannot carry an SQL payload

cons.claim: validation is not a substitute for context-correct encoding/parameterization and can give false safety
cons.example: validated text still breaks an HTML context without output encoding

acceptance_tests: each entry point validates against an allow-list schema
canonicalization precedes validation decisions
violations are rejected and logged
revisit_triggers: new input field or parameter type

nodes.definition: Prevent SQL/NoSQL injection by using parameterized queries and safe query builders, and detect injection attempts in logs and WAF rules.
contradictors: developer who concatenates user input into SQL

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect sql_injection_prevention

pros.claim: parameter binding structurally separates code from data so injection cannot alter query intent
pros.example: a bound :id parameter treats 1 OR 1=1 as a literal, not logic

cons.claim: dynamic identifiers (table/column names) and stored procs can reintroduce injection if not allow-listed
cons.example: an ORDER BY column taken from input bypasses binding

failure_modes: string-built queries remain in legacy paths
acceptance_tests: every query site uses parameter binding or an allow-listed identifier
no user input is concatenated into query text
injection probes are logged and detectable

nodes.definition: Prevent cross-site scripting via context-aware output encoding and safe templating, reinforced by Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth.
contradictors: developer who inserts raw user data into the DOM

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect xss_prevention_output_encoding

pros.claim: encoding chosen by output context neutralizes script injection at the exact sink
pros.example: encoding < as < in HTML context prevents tag injection

cons.claim: a single wrong-context or missed DOM sink reopens XSS despite broad coverage
cons.example: HTML-encoding data placed into a JS string still executes

acceptance_tests: each sink encodes for its actual output context
DOM sinks use safe APIs or sanitizers
reflected/stored probes do not execute
revisit_triggers: new rendering framework or template engine
new output context or rich-text feature

nodes.definition: Configure Content-Security-Policy and security headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy) to reduce exploitability and constrain injected content.
contradictors: team that ships unsafe-inline CSP to avoid refactoring

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect csp_and_security_headers

pros.claim: a strict CSP limits the blast radius of an XSS bug that slips through encoding
pros.example: nonce-based CSP blocks injected inline script even if a sink is missed

cons.claim: overly strict CSP breaks features and pressures teams toward unsafe-inline, weakening it
cons.example: a CDN widget forces a relaxed script-src that admits injection

acceptance_tests: CSP is enforced (not report-only) without unsafe-inline
frame-ancestors and HSTS present
violation reports are collected

nodes.definition: Implement robust authentication and session management: credential handling, session token issuance/expiry/rotation, and fixation/hijacking defenses.
contradictors: developer who stores session ids in URLs

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect authentication_and_session_management

pros.claim: correct session lifecycle prevents fixation, replay, and stale-session takeover
pros.example: rotating the session id on login defeats fixation

cons.claim: session controls interact with caching, SSO, and mobile clients and can break or be bypassed
cons.example: aggressive idle timeout pushes users to weaker 'remember me' tokens

acceptance_tests: session id rotates on privilege change and login
tokens expire and invalidate on logout
passwords stored with a strong adaptive hash
revisit_triggers: new client type or SSO integration

nodes.definition: Securely integrate OAuth 2.0 / OIDC: correct grant selection, redirect-URI and state/PKCE validation, token audience/scope handling, and provider trust.
contradictors: developer using implicit flow with wildcard redirect URIs

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect oauth_oidc_federated_identity

pros.claim: PKCE plus strict redirect/state validation blocks code interception and CSRF on the callback
pros.example: exact-match redirect URI prevents token exfiltration to attacker hosts

cons.claim: the spec has many insecure-but-legal options and provider quirks that invite misconfiguration
cons.example: accepting tokens without audience checks lets a token from another client be replayed

acceptance_tests: authorization-code flow with PKCE is enforced
redirect URIs are exact-match allow-listed
state/nonce and audience are validated

nodes.definition: Avoid JWT and bearer-token pitfalls: enforce algorithm and signature verification, audience/expiry claims, key management, and safe token storage.
contradictors: developer who trusts the alg header from the token

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect jwt_and_token_security

pros.claim: server-side alg allow-listing and signature verification defeats alg-confusion and forgery
pros.example: rejecting alg:none and verifying with the expected key blocks token forgery

cons.claim: tokens are bearer credentials: weak storage or no revocation makes theft fully exploitable
cons.example: an XSS-stolen JWT in localStorage grants full account access until expiry

failure_modes: tokens in localStorage exposed to XSS
acceptance_tests: signature and an allow-listed alg are verified server-side
aud/iss/exp/nbf are validated
a revocation or short-lived-token path exists

nodes.definition: Enforce server-side authorization on every request, defeating IDOR/BOLA, privilege escalation, and forced browsing through centralized, deny-by-default checks.
contradictors: developer who hides actions in the UI but not the API

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect broken_access_control_defense

pros.claim: server-side object-level checks stop attackers from accessing other users' resources by id swap
pros.example: verifying record ownership blocks GET /invoice/124 from user 123

cons.claim: authorization logic is scattered and context-dependent, so coverage gaps are common and silent
cons.example: a new bulk-export endpoint ships without the ownership check used elsewhere

acceptance_tests: every endpoint enforces server-side authz
object access verifies ownership/tenant
forced-browsing and id-swap tests fail to escalate

nodes.definition: Defend against cross-site request forgery using anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and origin/referer validation for state-changing requests.
contradictors: developer who relies on a custom header alone behind permissive CORS

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect csrf_defense

pros.claim: token plus SameSite binds a state-changing request to the user's own session and origin
pros.example: a per-session CSRF token absent from a forged cross-site POST causes rejection

cons.claim: SPA/API and CORS designs change which CSRF defense applies; a wrong assumption leaves a gap
cons.example: SameSite=None for a third-party widget reopens cross-site POST risk

acceptance_tests: state-changing requests require a validated anti-CSRF signal
cookies use an appropriate SameSite value
forged cross-site requests are rejected

nodes.definition: Prevent server-side request forgery by allow-listing outbound destinations, blocking internal/metadata ranges, and validating user-supplied URLs at fetch sinks.
contradictors: developer who fetches any user-supplied URL server-side

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect ssrf_defense

pros.claim: allow-listing egress and blocking link-local ranges stops pivoting to cloud metadata and internal services
pros.example: blocking 169.254.169.254 prevents credential theft from the metadata service

cons.claim: DNS rebinding, redirects, and IPv6/encoding tricks bypass naive URL filters
cons.example: a hostname that re-resolves to an internal IP after the check reaches internal services

acceptance_tests: outbound fetches use an allow-list and re-resolved IP checks
internal and metadata ranges are blocked
redirects are constrained or disabled

nodes.definition: Prevent insecure deserialization and unsafe object instantiation by avoiding native deserialization of untrusted data and constraining types and gadgets.

included: safe data formats over native serialization

contradictors: developer who deserializes user-controlled binary blobs

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect insecure_deserialization_defense

pros.claim: avoiding native deserialization of untrusted input removes RCE gadget-chain exposure
pros.example: switching from Java native serialization to schema-validated JSON eliminates the gadget sink

cons.claim: framework-default deserializers and transitive gadgets reintroduce risk invisibly
cons.example: a logging library on the classpath supplies a usable gadget chain

acceptance_tests: untrusted data uses safe, schema-validated formats
deserialization restricts types to an allow-list
payloads are integrity-checked

nodes.definition: Manage application secrets safely: centralized storage, no secrets in code or config, rotation, scoping, and leak detection.
contradictors: developer who commits API keys to the repository

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect secrets_management

pros.claim: centralized, rotated, scoped secrets limit blast radius and enable fast revocation on leak
pros.example: a leaked but narrowly-scoped, rotated key is revoked before broad abuse

cons.claim: secrets sprawl across CI, images, and logs, so a single missed location undoes the control
cons.example: a key printed to a build log persists in artifact storage

acceptance_tests: no secret is present in code, config, or logs
secrets are rotatable and scoped to least privilege
repo and pipeline secret scanning is enabled

nodes.definition: Harden transport security: enforce TLS with strong protocol/cipher configuration, HSTS, certificate validation, and no mixed or downgradable content.
contradictors: team serving an HTTPS site that still allows plaintext fallback

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect tls_and_transport_security

pros.claim: strong TLS plus HSTS prevents interception and downgrade of authenticated traffic
pros.example: HSTS preload stops an SSL-strip downgrade on first connection

cons.claim: certificate and protocol config drifts and pinning can cause outages if mismanaged
cons.example: an expired pin breaks mobile clients during rotation

acceptance_tests: only strong protocols/ciphers are accepted
HSTS is enforced with redirect-to-HTTPS
clients validate certificates correctly

nodes.definition: Detect and remediate vulnerable and malicious third-party components via software composition analysis, SBOM, and prioritized upgrade workflows.
contradictors: team that pins nothing and never patches transitive deps

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect dependency_and_sca_scanning

pros.claim: SCA surfaces known-vulnerable and malicious components before they ship and ranks fixes by reachability
pros.example: an SCA gate blocks a build pulling a log4j version with a known RCE

cons.claim: CVE noise and transitive depth cause alert fatigue and false-priority without reachability analysis
cons.example: hundreds of unreachable CVEs bury the one exploitable transitive dependency

acceptance_tests: builds produce an SBOM and run SCA
reachable high-severity findings block release
remediation is prioritized by exploitability

nodes.definition: Detect first-party vulnerabilities through static analysis, dynamic scanning, and security-focused code review integrated into the development pipeline.
contradictors: team that runs scanners but never triages findings

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect sast_dast_and_secure_code_review

pros.claim: layered SAST/DAST/review catches different vulnerability classes earlier than any single method
pros.example: DAST finds a runtime auth bypass SAST cannot see in source

cons.claim: high false-positive rates and poor triage erode trust and let real findings slip
cons.example: developers ignore a noisy SAST gate and miss a genuine injection finding

acceptance_tests: each method's findings are triaged to true/false positive
authenticated DAST covers privileged paths
confirmed findings become tracked remediation

nodes.definition: Instrument application-layer security logging and detection so authorized defenders can observe abuse, attacks, and anomalies without leaking sensitive data.
contradictors: team that logs nothing security-relevant at the app layer

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect security_logging_and_detection

pros.claim: logging authn failures, authz denials, and injection probes lets defenders detect attacks in progress
pros.example: a spike of authz-denied object-id sweeps reveals an IDOR-probing attacker

cons.claim: over-logging leaks secrets/PII and under-logging blinds detection; the balance is hard
cons.example: logging full request bodies captures passwords and tokens

acceptance_tests: security-relevant events are logged in a parseable schema
logs exclude secrets and PII
key abuse cases raise alerts
revisit_triggers: new abuse case or attack pattern

nodes.definition: Author and tune WAF and runtime-protection rules as defense in depth and virtual patching, scoped to complement (not replace) code-level fixes.
contradictors: team that treats a WAF as a substitute for fixing the code

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect waf_and_runtime_protection

pros.claim: a tuned WAF buys time via virtual patching and blocks commodity attacks while code is fixed
pros.example: a WAF rule blocks a mass-exploited path until the real patch ships

cons.claim: WAFs create false confidence and are bypassable, and false positives break legitimate traffic
cons.example: a normalization trick slips an injection past a signature the team trusted

acceptance_tests: WAF rules map to specific known risks
virtual patches are tracked to a code-fix backlog
bypass and FP rates are reviewed

nodes.definition: Prevent information disclosure through safe error handling, generic client responses, and suppression of stack traces, version banners, and verbose diagnostics.
contradictors: developer who returns raw exceptions to clients

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect error_handling_and_info_disclosure

pros.claim: generic errors deny attackers the oracle and recon that targeted exploitation relies on
pros.example: a generic 403 hides whether a record exists, blunting enumeration

cons.claim: over-generic errors hide real failures from defenders and degrade debuggability
cons.example: suppressing all detail also hides a misconfiguration from operators

acceptance_tests: client responses are generic and non-revealing
stack traces and debug modes are disabled in production
responses omit sensitive internals

nodes.definition: Defend against automated abuse and business-logic flaws via rate limiting, anti-automation, and workflow-integrity controls on sensitive operations.
contradictors: team that secures syntax but ignores workflow abuse

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect rate_limiting_and_business_logic_abuse

pros.claim: rate limits and invariant checks stop credential stuffing and logic abuse that pass per-request validation
pros.example: limiting login attempts per account slows credential-stuffing campaigns

cons.claim: aggressive limits harm legitimate users and logic invariants are app-specific and easy to miss
cons.example: a coupon-stacking flaw passes every input check yet drains revenue

failure_modes: no rate limit on sensitive operations
acceptance_tests: sensitive operations enforce rate limits server-side
key business invariants are validated server-side
abuse patterns raise alerts

nodes.definition: Track findings to remediation and enforce a risk-based security release gate so unresolved high-risk issues block or are explicitly accepted before deploy.
contradictors: team that ships with open critical findings and no record

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when new evidence, findings, or scope changes affect remediation_tracking_and_release_gate

pros.claim: a risk-based gate prevents shipping known high-risk vulnerabilities and records accountable exceptions
pros.example: an unfixed critical SQLi finding blocks release until patched or formally accepted

cons.claim: rigid gates create pressure to under-classify or bypass, hiding real risk behind green checks
cons.example: a critical bug is downgraded to 'medium' to clear the gate before a deadline

acceptance_tests: every high-risk finding is fixed, retested, or formally accepted before release
release decisions are recorded with risk acceptance
fixes are verified by retest

edges.why_related: validation targets the entry points and trust boundaries the threat model identifies
edges.benefit_of_coupling: scope-driven validation avoids gaps and wasted effort
edges.risk_of_conflict: validating without a model leaves entry points uncovered
edges.example: an unmodeled API skips validation
edges.resolution_rule: define scope before authoring validation rules

edges.why_related: authorization needs the asset, role, and tenant model from threat modeling
edges.benefit_of_coupling: scoped authz covers every protected object and function
edges.risk_of_conflict: authz built without a model misses objects
edges.example: a sharing feature absent from the model ships unauthorized
edges.resolution_rule: model assets and roles before authz design

edges.why_related: authentication requirements derive from the trust boundaries in scope
edges.benefit_of_coupling: right authn strength is chosen per boundary
edges.risk_of_conflict: unscoped authn over/under-protects boundaries
edges.example: an internal admin path lacks step-up auth
edges.resolution_rule: scope trust boundaries before authn design

edges.why_related: parameterization assumes inputs are already normalized and constrained
edges.benefit_of_coupling: clean inputs reduce edge cases at the query layer
edges.risk_of_conflict: unnormalized input complicates safe queries
edges.example: an un-canonicalized id reaches the data layer
edges.resolution_rule: normalize/validate input before query construction

edges.why_related: validation reduces but does not replace context encoding at output
edges.benefit_of_coupling: fewer malformed values reach the encoder
edges.risk_of_conflict: treating validation as sufficient reopens XSS
edges.example: validated text still breaks a JS context
edges.resolution_rule: validate input AND encode at output; never one alone

edges.why_related: SSRF URL checks depend on canonicalized, validated URL inputs
edges.benefit_of_coupling: normalized URLs make allow-listing reliable
edges.risk_of_conflict: raw URLs enable parser-confusion bypasses
edges.example: an encoded URL bypasses a naive check
edges.resolution_rule: canonicalize URLs before allow-list checks

edges.why_related: deserialization safety builds on constraining untrusted input formats
edges.benefit_of_coupling: constrained formats shrink the deserialization surface
edges.risk_of_conflict: unconstrained blobs feed unsafe deserializers
edges.example: a binary blob field is deserialized natively
edges.resolution_rule: constrain input formats before deserialization

edges.why_related: CSP is defense-in-depth layered after correct output encoding
edges.benefit_of_coupling: CSP limits blast radius of any missed encoding
edges.risk_of_conflict: relying on CSP alone leaves root-cause XSS
edges.example: unsafe-inline CSP masks an unencoded sink
edges.resolution_rule: fix encoding first; add CSP as a backstop

edges.why_related: federated flows extend the session and credential model
edges.benefit_of_coupling: consistent identity from auth foundation
edges.risk_of_conflict: OAuth bolted on without session rules conflicts
edges.example: an OIDC login leaves a non-rotated session
edges.resolution_rule: establish session model before federation

edges.why_related: token validation rules depend on the chosen OAuth/OIDC flow and provider keys
edges.benefit_of_coupling: correct flow yields verifiable tokens
edges.risk_of_conflict: tokens validated without flow context are forgeable
edges.example: an audience-less token is accepted cross-client
edges.resolution_rule: define flow and keys before token validation

edges.why_related: authorization decisions require an authenticated, trustworthy identity
edges.benefit_of_coupling: authz binds to a verified principal
edges.risk_of_conflict: authz over a weak identity is meaningless
edges.example: an unrotated session id enables authz under a hijacked identity
edges.resolution_rule: stabilize authentication before authorization

edges.why_related: CSRF defenses bind state-changing actions to the established session
edges.benefit_of_coupling: session-bound tokens reject forged requests
edges.risk_of_conflict: CSRF design without a session model is incoherent
edges.example: SameSite choice conflicts with the cookie model
edges.resolution_rule: fix session/cookie model before CSRF tokens

edges.why_related: authorization bounds which forged actions even matter for CSRF
edges.benefit_of_coupling: authz limits CSRF impact to permitted actions
edges.risk_of_conflict: assuming CSRF alone covers authz is wrong
edges.example: a CSRF token passes but authz still denies
edges.resolution_rule: authz and CSRF are separate controls; keep both

edges.why_related: abuse and logic controls operate within the authorization model
edges.benefit_of_coupling: limits apply per authorized principal/object
edges.risk_of_conflict: rate limits without authz context misattribute abuse
edges.example: a shared key evades per-user limits
edges.resolution_rule: define authz before per-principal abuse limits

edges.why_related: SSRF egress allow-lists depend on the internal network map from scoping
edges.benefit_of_coupling: accurate internal map yields tight egress rules
edges.risk_of_conflict: unmapped internal services stay reachable
edges.example: metadata endpoint omitted from the block map
edges.resolution_rule: map internal/egress targets before SSRF rules

edges.why_related: secret scoping depends on knowing which assets and trust boundaries need them
edges.benefit_of_coupling: scoped secrets follow the trust map
edges.risk_of_conflict: unscoped secrets over-grant access
edges.example: a broad key spans unrelated boundaries
edges.resolution_rule: scope secrets to modeled trust boundaries

edges.why_related: detection signals are derived from the abuse cases enumerated in scoping
edges.benefit_of_coupling: abuse-case-driven logging catches real attacks
edges.risk_of_conflict: logging without abuse cases misses signals
edges.example: an unmodeled attack leaves no detection
edges.resolution_rule: derive detection from modeled abuse cases

edges.why_related: WAF rules are tuned against logged traffic and detection signals
edges.benefit_of_coupling: telemetry informs precise WAF rules
edges.risk_of_conflict: WAF rules without telemetry are blind
edges.example: a rule blocks legit traffic seen in logs
edges.resolution_rule: build logging/detection before tuning WAF

edges.why_related: rich server logging aids defenders but verbose client errors aid attackers
edges.benefit_of_coupling: separating log verbosity from client output serves both
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them either blinds defenders or leaks to attackers
edges.example: a stack trace shown to the user is also the only log
edges.resolution_rule: log verbosely server-side; return generic errors to clients

edges.why_related: CSP violation reports reveal missed encoding sinks to revisit
edges.benefit_of_coupling: reports drive root-cause encoding fixes
edges.risk_of_conflict: treating CSP reports as the fix leaves the sink
edges.example: a recurring CSP report flags an unencoded widget
edges.resolution_rule: use CSP reports to trigger encoding fixes; stop when the sink is remediated and reports cease

edges.why_related: both are vulnerability-detection workstreams over different code surfaces
edges.benefit_of_coupling: shared triage and routing reduce duplicate effort
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them leaves first- or third-party gaps
edges.example: an SCA finding is mistaken for a SAST finding
edges.resolution_rule: keep SCA (deps) and SAST/DAST (first-party) as distinct but coordinated detection

edges.why_related: the gate consumes triaged first-party findings to decide release
edges.benefit_of_coupling: verified findings drive gate decisions
edges.risk_of_conflict: ungated findings ship unfixed
edges.example: a confirmed SQLi never reaches the gate
edges.resolution_rule: triage findings before the release gate

edges.why_related: the gate consumes reachable SCA findings for release decisions
edges.benefit_of_coupling: reachable CVEs are gated, not ignored
edges.risk_of_conflict: unreachable-noise floods the gate
edges.example: a reachable RCE CVE bypasses the gate
edges.resolution_rule: feed reachability-triaged SCA findings to the gate

edges.why_related: access-control defects are high-severity inputs to the release gate
edges.benefit_of_coupling: authz gaps block release until fixed
edges.risk_of_conflict: an IDOR ships behind a green gate
edges.example: a bulk-export IDOR escapes the gate
edges.resolution_rule: treat authz defects as gate-blocking high risk

edges.why_related: both protect confidentiality of credentials/keys in storage and transit
edges.benefit_of_coupling: coordinated key and transport hygiene
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them leaves storage or transit weak
edges.example: a key is rotated but sent over weak TLS
edges.resolution_rule: keep secret storage and transport hardening as complementary controls

edges.why_related: validation rejections must produce safe, generic errors
edges.benefit_of_coupling: clean rejection avoids leaking validation internals
edges.risk_of_conflict: verbose rejections become an enumeration oracle
edges.example: a validation error reveals the backend regex
edges.resolution_rule: return generic errors on validation failure

edges.why_related: injection attempts should be logged for detection even when blocked
edges.benefit_of_coupling: blocked-attempt telemetry reveals targeting
edges.risk_of_conflict: silent blocking loses attacker visibility
edges.example: an injection probe is parameter-safe but unlogged
edges.resolution_rule: log injection probes even when parameterization blocks them

edges.why_related: authorization denials are primary detection signals for probing
edges.benefit_of_coupling: denial telemetry surfaces IDOR sweeps
edges.risk_of_conflict: unlogged denials hide enumeration
edges.example: an id-sweep produces denials no one sees
edges.resolution_rule: log authz denials as detection signals

edges.why_related: token validation failures are useful detection signals
edges.benefit_of_coupling: failed-verify telemetry flags forgery attempts
edges.risk_of_conflict: silent token rejection loses signal
edges.example: an alg:none attempt is rejected but unlogged
edges.resolution_rule: log token verification failures for detection

edges.why_related: OAuth scopes constrain but do not replace server-side authorization
edges.benefit_of_coupling: scopes plus authz give layered control
edges.risk_of_conflict: trusting scopes alone leaves object-level gaps
edges.example: a valid scope still must pass ownership checks
edges.resolution_rule: treat scopes as coarse limits; enforce object-level authz server-side

edges.why_related: a WAF can virtually patch injection but must not displace the parameterization fix
edges.benefit_of_coupling: WAF buys time while code is fixed
edges.risk_of_conflict: relying on the WAF leaves the root cause
edges.example: a WAF block is treated as the SQLi remediation
edges.resolution_rule: WAF is temporary mitigation; the parameterization fix dominates and must still ship

edges.why_related: WAF XSS signatures are bypassable and must not replace output encoding
edges.benefit_of_coupling: WAF blocks commodity XSS while encoding is fixed
edges.risk_of_conflict: WAF false confidence leaves DOM-XSS open
edges.example: a WAF rule is treated as the XSS fix
edges.resolution_rule: encoding is the root fix; WAF is a bypassable backstop, never the resolution

edges.why_related: both are response/transport hardening controls configured at the platform edge
edges.benefit_of_coupling: coordinated edge hardening
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them leaves header or transport gaps
edges.example: HSTS set but a weak cipher allowed
edges.resolution_rule: keep header and TLS hardening as distinct platform controls

edges.why_related: gate outcomes and new findings feed back to revise the threat model
edges.benefit_of_coupling: real findings sharpen the model's abuse cases
edges.risk_of_conflict: ignoring gate feedback freezes a stale model
edges.example: a recurring class of findings is never modeled
edges.resolution_rule: feed release-gate findings back into the threat model; stop when the model covers the observed class

edges.why_related: abuse controls depend on monitoring to detect and tune thresholds
edges.benefit_of_coupling: abuse telemetry tunes limits
edges.risk_of_conflict: blind limits over/under-block
edges.example: credential stuffing is throttled but untracked
edges.resolution_rule: log abuse signals to tune rate limits

edges.why_related: gadget-chain risk is bounded by which vulnerable dependencies are present
edges.benefit_of_coupling: SCA reveals gadget-providing libraries
edges.risk_of_conflict: ignoring deps hides reachable gadgets
edges.example: a logging lib adds an exploitable gadget
edges.resolution_rule: use SCA to bound deserialization gadget surface

edges.why_related: both reduce attacker information and exploitability at the response layer
edges.benefit_of_coupling: coordinated response hardening
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them leaves headers or errors leaky
edges.example: a debug banner persists despite strict CSP
edges.resolution_rule: keep header hardening and error suppression as complementary response controls

conflict_axes.trigger: strict timeouts, limits, and step-up auth degrade legitimate user experience
resolution_order: set controls by data sensitivity and risk
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for high-sensitivity operations security strength dominates; for low-risk flows minimize friction with adaptive controls
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a control blocks a material fraction of legitimate users
conflict_axes.example: forcing re-authentication on every action to prevent session replay

conflict_axes.trigger: a mitigating control creates pressure to defer or skip the underlying code fix
resolution_order: track the root-cause fix as required
retire the virtual patch after the fix
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: the root-cause fix dominates; mitigations are temporary and must not close the remediation ticket
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a virtual patch persists past its remediation SLA
conflict_axes.example: treating a WAF SQLi signature as the permanent remediation

conflict_axes.trigger: verbose diagnostics help defenders but the same detail helps attackers if returned to clients
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: defenders get full server-side detail; clients get generic responses; neither side is sacrificed
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if logs capture credentials/PII or clients receive stack traces
conflict_axes.example: echoing a backend stack trace to the user as the only error record

conflict_axes.trigger: treating input validation as the complete defense omits context-correct encoding/parameterization
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: sink-side encoding/parameterization is mandatory regardless of validation; validation is complementary, not a substitute
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if any sink relies on validation alone for safety
conflict_axes.example: assuming a validated field is safe to drop unencoded into HTML

conflict_axes.trigger: a security gate blocks a release deadline when high-risk findings remain open
resolution_order: block or formally accept high risk
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: risk-based gating dominates schedule for high-risk findings; exceptions require explicit, recorded acceptance
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a critical finding is downgraded to clear the gate
conflict_axes.example: reclassifying a critical SQLi as medium to ship on time

conflict_axes.trigger: broad scanning raises coverage but floods triage with false positives and unreachable findings
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: reachable, exploitable findings dominate; coverage is tuned to preserve signal over raw volume
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if real findings are ignored due to alert fatigue
conflict_axes.example: hundreds of unreachable CVEs burying one exploitable dependency

conflict_axes.trigger: aggressive blocking and throttling reduce attack surface but can deny service to legitimate users
resolution_order: tune thresholds to minimize false blocks
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for confirmed attack patterns blocking dominates; for ambiguous traffic prefer monitoring/alerting over outright denial
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if blocking measurably harms legitimate availability
conflict_axes.example: a strict WAF rule blocking a legitimate bulk API client

conflict_axes.trigger: trusting external IdP scopes/claims can substitute for, and weaken, server-side authorization
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: server-side authorization dominates; federated claims are coarse inputs, never the final access decision
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if access is granted on scope alone without ownership checks
conflict_axes.example: granting record access because a valid scoped token was presented

conflict_axes.trigger: strict CSP/TLS/header policies break third-party widgets, legacy clients, or features
resolution_order: promote to enforce without unsafe directives
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: enforced hardening dominates once violations are remediated; compatibility is addressed by fixing causes, not relaxing the policy
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if compatibility pressure forces unsafe-inline or weak ciphers
conflict_axes.example: adding unsafe-inline to CSP so a vendor script keeps working

edge_cases.trigger: validation uses a blocklist instead of an allow-list
edge_cases.failure_mode: encoding/obfuscation bypasses the filter and reaches a sink
edge_cases.example: a double-encoded payload slips past a denylist into a query path
edge_cases.detection_method: audit validation rules for deny-list patterns and fuzz with encoded variants
resolution: ensure sink-side parameterization regardless of validation

edge_cases.trigger: data encoded for one context is placed into another
edge_cases.failure_mode: XSS executes despite encoding being applied
edge_cases.example: HTML-encoded value inserted inside a JavaScript string still runs
edge_cases.detection_method: map each sink to its output context and verify the encoder matches
resolution: apply context-correct encoding at each sink
review DOM sinks for safe APIs

edge_cases.trigger: a new endpoint ships without the object-level ownership check used elsewhere
edge_cases.failure_mode: IDOR/BOLA lets a user access another user's resource
edge_cases.example: GET /export/{id} returns records owned by other tenants
edge_cases.detection_method: run authorization test matrix (id-swap, forced browsing) against every endpoint

edge_cases.trigger: the server trusts the token's alg header or accepts alg:none
edge_cases.example: an RS256 verifier tricked into HS256 using the public key as the HMAC secret
edge_cases.detection_method: test tokens with alg:none and swapped algorithms against verification
resolution: verify with the correct key type

edge_cases.trigger: loose redirect-uri matching or missing state validation
edge_cases.failure_mode: authorization code or token is exfiltrated to an attacker host
edge_cases.example: a wildcard redirect URI sends the code to attacker.example
edge_cases.detection_method: test callback with mismatched/extra redirect URIs and missing state

edge_cases.trigger: URL validated then fetched, allowing DNS rebinding or redirect to internal IPs
edge_cases.failure_mode: server reaches internal services or cloud metadata
edge_cases.example: a hostname re-resolving to 169.254.169.254 after the check
edge_cases.detection_method: test with rebinding hosts, redirects, and internal/metadata targets
resolution: re-resolve and check the final IP at fetch time

edge_cases.trigger: a credential is committed to source or printed to a build log
edge_cases.failure_mode: leaked secret enables unauthorized access until rotated
edge_cases.example: an API key in a committed .env file in git history
edge_cases.detection_method: run repo and pipeline secret scanning across history and logs

edge_cases.trigger: a WAF block is recorded as the remediation for a code-level flaw
edge_cases.failure_mode: root cause persists and is reachable via WAF bypass
edge_cases.example: closing a SQLi ticket because a WAF signature blocks the known payload
edge_cases.detection_method: cross-check WAF mitigations against an open code-fix backlog
resolution: keep the code-fix ticket open until parameterized
treat WAF as temporary virtual patch

edge_cases.trigger: native deserialization of untrusted data with gadget-rich dependencies
edge_cases.failure_mode: remote code execution via a gadget chain
edge_cases.example: a serialized object triggers a chain through a logging library on the classpath
edge_cases.detection_method: inventory deserialization sinks and scan deps for known gadgets

edge_cases.trigger: compatibility pressure forces unsafe-inline into CSP
edge_cases.failure_mode: CSP no longer mitigates injected inline script
edge_cases.example: a vendor widget requires inline scripts so the policy admits all inline
edge_cases.detection_method: audit CSP for unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval and inline-script usage
resolution: keep encoding as the root defense

edge_cases.trigger: high false-positive volume erodes trust in scanner output
edge_cases.failure_mode: a real exploitable finding is ignored amid noise
edge_cases.example: developers mute a noisy SAST gate and miss a genuine injection
edge_cases.detection_method: track false-positive rate and time-to-triage per tool

edge_cases.trigger: detection logging captures full requests including credentials or PII
edge_cases.failure_mode: logs become a new sensitive-data exposure surface
edge_cases.example: logging full POST bodies records plaintext passwords
edge_cases.detection_method: scan log schema and samples for secrets/PII fields
resolution: log security events, not raw payloads

workflow.objective: scope the attack surface, trust boundaries, and abuse cases
acceptance_tests: every external entry point is modeled
each trust boundary names its authz check
exit_criteria: threat model reviewed and scope agreed
workflow.do_first_because: all testing, hardening, and detection scope inherit from the threat model

workflow.objective: define allow-list validation and canonicalization at boundaries
acceptance_tests: each entry point validates against an allow-list
canonicalization precedes validation
exit_criteria: validation rules defined for all entry points
workflow.do_first_because: downstream injection defenses assume normalized, constrained inputs

workflow.objective: establish authentication, session, and token security
acceptance_tests: session id rotates on login/privilege change
tokens are signature- and claim-verified
workflow.do_first_because: authorization and CSRF defenses depend on a trustworthy identity

workflow.objective: enforce server-side authorization and request integrity
acceptance_tests: id-swap and forced-browsing tests fail to escalate
forged cross-site requests are rejected
workflow.do_first_because: broken access control is the highest-impact, easily-overlooked class

acceptance_tests: no input is concatenated into queries
each sink encodes for its context
outbound fetches use allow-listed IPs
workflow.do_first_because: injection classes are high-severity and broadly exploitable

workflow.objective: harden response, transport, secrets, and abuse resistance as defense in depth
acceptance_tests: CSP enforced without unsafe-inline
only strong TLS accepted
no secret in code/config/logs
workflow.do_first_because: hardening reduces blast radius when a primary control fails

workflow.objective: instrument detection and runtime protection for authorized defenders
acceptance_tests: key abuse cases raise alerts
logs exclude secrets/PII
workflow.do_first_because: detection turns residual risk into observable, actionable signal

workflow.objective: detect first- and third-party vulnerabilities via scanning and review
acceptance_tests: findings triaged to true/false positive
reachable high-severity issues identified
workflow.do_first_because: verification confirms which modeled risks are actually present

workflow.objective: track remediation and enforce a risk-based release gate
acceptance_tests: high-risk findings are fixed, retested, or formally accepted
exceptions are recorded with risk acceptance
workflow.do_first_because: no high-risk issue should ship without remediation or accountable acceptance

workflow.objective: feed findings and detections back to revise the model and controls
entry_criteria: a release cycle completed or new finding/detection received
acceptance_tests: new finding classes are reflected in the model
revalidation passes after changes
exit_criteria: model and controls updated and revalidated
workflow.do_first_because: continuous feedback keeps the model and detections aligned with real attacks

identity foundation for authz and CSRF
token forgery is auth bypass; high risk
high-severity injection with clean structural fix
broadly exploitable; root fix before CSP
binds state changes to session; after identity
leaks are hard to fully reverse; scope and rotate

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-risk vulnerability conflicts with a release deadline
dominance_rules.rule: remediating high-risk vulnerabilities dominates schedule pressure
dominance_rules.required_action: fix, retest, or formally accept high-risk findings before release
dominance_rules.example: shipping an open critical SQLi to meet a date

dominance_rules.trigger: a WAF/CSP mitigation is offered as a substitute for the code fix
dominance_rules.rule: the root-cause code fix dominates temporary mitigations
dominance_rules.required_action: keep the code-fix ticket open until remediated; retire the virtual patch after
dominance_rules.example: closing a SQLi bug because a WAF blocks the payload

dominance_rules.trigger: UI hides an action but the API does not enforce authorization
dominance_rules.required_action: enforce authorization on every request server-side
dominance_rules.example: relying on a hidden button to prevent an action

dominance_rules.trigger: input validation is treated as sufficient without sink encoding/parameterization
dominance_rules.rule: context encoding/parameterization at the sink dominates validation-only defense
dominance_rules.required_action: encode/parameterize at every sink regardless of validation
dominance_rules.example: dropping a validated value unencoded into HTML

dominance_rules.trigger: a finding involves irreversible action, exploitation framing, or high risk
dominance_rules.rule: human review dominates automation for high-risk or irreversible security decisions
dominance_rules.required_action: require human sign-off before finalizing high-risk or irreversible changes
dominance_rules.example: auto-accepting a risk exception for a critical finding

dominance_rules.trigger: attacker knowledge could be framed as an operational exploitation playbook
dominance_rules.rule: offense-aware DEFENSE framing dominates; attacker knowledge serves detection and hardening only
dominance_rules.required_action: frame all attacker knowledge as detection/prevention guidance for authorized systems
dominance_rules.example: writing a step-by-step exploit for an unauthorized target

dominance_rules.trigger: a numeric score implies more certainty than the heuristic evidence supports
dominance_rules.required_action: label heuristic estimates as heuristic; do not assert observed certainty
dominance_rules.example: presenting a heuristic risk as a measured rate

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-value control is sequenced before an unmet prerequisite
dominance_rules.required_action: order work by true prerequisites before risk-adjusted value
dominance_rules.example: building authz before a trustworthy identity exists

dominance_rules.trigger: a control is about to be hard-locked before its acceptance tests pass
dominance_rules.rule: QA and validation dominate locking progress
dominance_rules.required_action: pass acceptance tests and gates before any hard lock
dominance_rules.example: hard-locking a release gate with failing authz tests

dominance_rules.trigger: verbose diagnostics would be exposed to clients to aid debugging
dominance_rules.rule: server-side detection logging dominates client-facing verbosity
dominance_rules.required_action: log detail on the server; return generic errors to clients
dominance_rules.example: echoing a stack trace to the user for convenience

anti_rework_rules.rule: scope the threat model before designing controls
anti_rework_rules.rationale: controls built without scope leave blind spots that are reworked later
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a shipped control misses an unmodeled entry point
anti_rework_rules.example: adding validation only after an endpoint is breached

anti_rework_rules.rule: define input normalization before relying on sink defenses
anti_rework_rules.rationale: un-normalized input causes sink-defense edge cases and rework
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a parser-confusion bypass surfaces after sink hardening
anti_rework_rules.example: hardening queries while raw input still varies in encoding

anti_rework_rules.rule: stabilize authentication and session before authorization
anti_rework_rules.rationale: authz over a weak identity must be reworked once identity changes
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: authz logic rewritten after a session model change
anti_rework_rules.example: writing ownership checks before sessions rotate correctly

anti_rework_rules.rule: choose the OAuth/OIDC flow before fixing token validation
anti_rework_rules.rationale: token rules depend on flow and keys; premature rules get redone
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: token validation rewritten after switching grant types
anti_rework_rules.example: validating tokens before the redirect/PKCE design is set

anti_rework_rules.rule: enforce server-side authorization before exposing new resource endpoints
anti_rework_rules.rationale: retrofitting authz onto shipped endpoints is costly and error-prone
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a new endpoint ships without the standard ownership check
anti_rework_rules.example: adding object-level checks only after an IDOR report

anti_rework_rules.rule: fix output encoding before relying on CSP
anti_rework_rules.rationale: CSP that masks unencoded sinks gives false safety and rework
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a CSP report keeps flagging the same unencoded widget
anti_rework_rules.example: shipping unsafe-inline CSP instead of fixing the sink

anti_rework_rules.rule: triage scanner findings before the release gate decides
anti_rework_rules.rationale: untriaged findings cause gate churn and ignored real risk
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: the gate blocks on false positives or passes on real ones
anti_rework_rules.example: gating on raw scanner output without reachability

anti_rework_rules.rule: retest a fix before locking the release gate
anti_rework_rules.rationale: locking before verification ships unverified or regressed fixes
anti_rework_rules.example: closing a finding without re-running the exploit-class test

anti_rework_rules.rule: remove secrets from code and pipelines before deploy
blocked_until: no secret in code, config, or logs
anti_rework_rules.rationale: secrets shipped to artifacts require rotation and history rewrites
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a build log or image contains a live key
anti_rework_rules.example: deploying with an API key in the repository

anti_rework_rules.rule: instrument detection for top abuse cases before release
anti_rework_rules.rationale: shipping without detection blinds defenders and delays response
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: an attack proceeds with no security log or alert
anti_rework_rules.example: releasing a feature with no authz-denial logging

iteration_protocol.trigger: a validator, scanner, or review reports a failure
acceptance_tests: every failure mapped to a subsystem

iteration_protocol.trigger: multiple defects compete for limited remediation effort
acceptance_tests: highest-risk exploitable defects ranked first
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: queue ordered and high-risk items addressed

iteration_protocol.trigger: a change touches a high-coupling or high-irreversibility control
iteration_protocol.detection: trace dependency and downstream edges from the changed node
acceptance_tests: all affected controls identified

iteration_protocol.trigger: a classified defect needs an owning subsystem
acceptance_tests: every defect has an owner

iteration_protocol.trigger: a fix or control change was applied
iteration_protocol.detection: re-run validators, scanners, and acceptance tests
acceptance_tests: previously failing checks now pass; no regressions
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: revalidation passes with no new failures

iteration_protocol.trigger: new evidence or findings change a node's importance
iteration_protocol.detection: compare posterior_importance shift to revisit delta
acceptance_tests: posterior recomputed within tolerance
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: posterior change below the revisit delta

iteration_protocol.trigger: a high-risk or irreversible decision exceeds automation authority
iteration_protocol.detection: check risk and irreversibility against review thresholds
acceptance_tests: human sign-off recorded for the decision
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: human review recorded or risk below threshold

iteration_protocol.trigger: a control, schema, or model version changes
iteration_protocol.detection: compare against the prior version's results
acceptance_tests: no security regressions vs prior version
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: no regression detected or regression repaired
